extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of natural philosophy and natural theology (learned laypeople, students, and scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: An early-modern natural-philosophy treatment of the structure and function of the ear (external ear, auditory tube, tympanum, ossicles, labyrinth, nerves) with experimental demonstrations and theological inferences about design. The text explains anatomical parts, their mechanical relations, experiments showing sound transmission, and arguments from those facts toward divine wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure sufficient to prove the Wisdom of the Creator
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Structure thereof, as far as it has hitherto been discovered, is sufficient to prove the wonderful Wisdom of the Creator”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial claim that the discovered anatomical arrangement of hearing instruments (even if not all uses are known) provides strong evidence of design; addressed as an inference that should convince an enquiring mind or an atheist unless obstinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilateral placement indicates design
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument from the fact that two ears are placed upon the head and animals turn the cavity of an ear toward a sound-source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence of purposive design because bilateral placement aids directional hearing and compensation (e.g., people cup hand behind ear when one ear fails); thus placement and behavior are taken as functional and not accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: External ear composition (membranes + cartilage) as functional design
rubrics_metrics.description: “the said whole Ear of Membranes supported with Cartilages ... endowed with an Elastick Faculty ... to redreſs itſelf”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why ear tissue is neither only soft (would hang and hinder hearing) nor only hard/bony (would cause inconvenience); elasticity allows restoration after bending and perhaps aids tremulous motion—an example of morphological fit to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory tube and tympanum arrangement for admitting and trapping sonoriferous air
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of auditory tube (cartilaginous near external, bony further in) and drum membrane that shuts end of tube, compelling sonoriferous air to run into it and strike the membrane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes observational note (tobacco smoke passing from mouth through ears) as possible evidence of an orifice; frames the drum membrane as the interface where air motion is converted to membrane motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tympanal cavity with ossicles transmits membrane motion mechanically
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cavity (tympanum) containing four little bones (hammer, anvil, stirrup) and the chorda tympani; the membrane's motion is communicated to these bones and the little nerve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the mechanical chain: drum membrane moves → hammer moves → anvil → fourth bone → stirrup; the chorda follows motions. This mechanical linkage is offered as evidence of an organized transmission system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openings (Eustachian tube/trumpet of Eustachius) serve pressure equalization and acoustic passage
rubrics_metrics.description: The tube (trumpet of Eustachius) terminates in the roof of the mouth so air passing through it enters the cavity of the drum; when stopped, the ear becomes immediately deaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental/observational guidance: stopping this orifice causes deafness; conversely, opening it restores hearing. Also used to explain conduction of sound via the mouth (e.g., holding a stick between teeth to transfer vibrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oval and round windows mediate transmission between tympanum and inner ear
rubrics_metrics.description: Two openings in the circumference of the drum's cavity: the Oval Window stopped by the stirrup and the Round Window closed by a membrane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes functional arrangement that allows the stirrup to move in the oval window and the round window to be relieved by a membrane—part of the path by which ossicle motion transmits to the inner labyrinth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labyrinth (semicircular canals, cochlea, vestibule) as inner apparatus for hearing and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The innermost cavity ('Labyrinth') contains three semicircular vessels, the cochlea (snail) and the vestibule; these structures and their membranes/partitions propagate tremulous motion of sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives morphological details (cochlea divided by septum into two tubes, different material properties) and indicates how these parts are suited to propagate vibratory motion toward auditory nerves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory nerves expand into membranes that form sensory surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory nerve divides into branches which pass into the vestibule and are expanded to compose its membrane; other branches enter the semicircular vessels forming membranes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents the nerves' expansion into membranous surfaces as the instruments actually affected by motion—i.e., the nerve-derived membranes are where hearing is formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory tube and cochlea function as a natural speaking horn to increase sound
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage through the cochlea and auditory tube (a natural speaking horn) strikes more strongly upon the drum membrane than sound striking without passing through such a tube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental demonstration: using a speaking trumpet (long conical tube) one can hear whispers clearly at the narrow end; deaf people using tubes with large mouth and narrow ear end can hear better—evidence that the tube amplifies sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound causes tremulous motion of membranes (demonstrable experimentally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds produce a tremulous motion in the drum membrane, analogous to vibrating bells, strings, or a drinking-glass; experiments with a glass, water, and finger demonstrate visible tremor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides experimental analogies and a constructed experiment using a trumpet covered by a bladder with feathers to show air vibrations produce tremulous motion felt and seen; establishes vibration as a mechanism of sound transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of ossicles transmits vibration into inner ear fluids and membranes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hammer motion moves anvil and stirrup; stirrup (closing the oval orifice) moves and by that motion the air and membranes of the vestibule and cochlea are set into motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how ossicular motion causes movement of air in the inner cavities and thereby excites membranes within semicircular canals and cochlea—linking external vibration to inner sensory activation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathological observations support functional assignments (ossification, drum rupture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that when the membrane around the stirrup was found to be all bone and the stirrup immovable, deafness resulted; drum membrane rupture does not cause immediate hearing loss but later corruption of other instruments does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses pathological findings to infer which parts are essential or secondary; immobility of ossicles causes deafness (supports their role), while drum membrane damage has delayed effect—used as diagnostic evidence for function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental constancy of auditory bones as evidence of design
rubrics_metrics.description: The little bones of hearing are of the very same size in a child as in a grown man, unlike other bones which grow with the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: constancy preserves familiar voice and sounds to children as they grow; used as teleological evidence that hearing structures are deliberately maintained to serve consistent auditory perception across ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective glands, viscous matter, and hairs in auditory tube serve maintenance and defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory tube is encompassed with small glands producing viscous yellow matter and has little hairs; the matter preserves moisture, stops insects and filth from entering, and prevents the tube from becoming too dry or too soft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional explanation of ancillary features: secretions keep the tube in a proper state, hairs and viscosity bar insects; these are cited as further evidence of wise provisioning of the organ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small muscles adjust ossicles to modulate hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Small muscles attached near the stirrup and hammer can stretch or relax, changing the position or tension of membranes and ossicles to render them more serviceable to the motion of sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes muscular control (e.g., a muscle which can move the head of the stirrup) as a regulatory mechanism, refining the ear's response to sound—another functional detail supporting purposive design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labyrinth nervous membranes are the place where hearing is formed
rubrics_metrics.description: The nervous membranes in all cavities and tubes of the labyrinth seem to be the instruments by which, and the labyrinth the place where, the hearing is formed because sound motion affects the auditory nerves or membranes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concludes from anatomical distribution and mutual motions that the final sensation arises in the labyrinth's nerve-derived membranes—synthesis of preceding anatomical and experimental observations into a site-of-sensation claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative functional complexity supports inference to design over chance
rubrics_metrics.description: The many appropriately arranged parts (shapes, sizes, connections, protections, and developmental features) make it unreasonable to ascribe the ear's structure to chance or ignorant causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical/theological guidance: invites an unbeliever to consider the assembly of features (mechanical, protective, developmental) and to judge whether attributing them to design or to fortuitous causes is more reasonable; uses multiple lines of anatomical and experimental evidence in the inference.
